Unity URP , View on GitHub Why I wanted to get hands-on with real-time rendering beyond "using shaders" - specifically: how procedural textures, custom shading, and world-space masks can be composed into a readable VFX sequence. This was my final project for CSCI 580: 3D Graphics and Rendering (USC, Fall 2025), where we explored both offline and realtime rendering techniques (rasterization, shading, noise/procedural generation, and pipeline concepts). What A real-time asteroid impact sequence in Unity URP: a procedural asteroid falls onto a terrain, an "impact frame" post-process sells the moment of collision, and an expanding shockwave reveals molten cracks across the ground. Procedural lava & cracks shader (HLSL): Built a terrain material that blends from normal ground to molten lava using 3D Worley noise for organic crack boundaries. Corner rounding for Worley junctions: Standard Worley borders can create sharp, unnatural corners at cell junctions. I used the third-nearest distance (F3) to compute a corner metric and widen cracks near junctions, producing rounded lava "veins." Outcomes Team system context This was a 4-person project. While I focused on terrain transformation, the full sequence also includes: Procedural asteroid generation (vertex displacement + heightfield-driven normals) Velocity-reactive asteroid lighting (emission + Fresnel rim "burn") Impact frame post-processing (edge detection + radial blur + polar noise "speed lines") Shockwave bubble shader (depth intersection + Fresnel + heat distortion) What worked well Readable, stylized “lava reveal”: The world-space mask + Worley cracks made the shockwave feel like it physically alters the terrain. More natural crack topology: Corner rounding reduced sharp triangular junctions common in basic Worley borders. Reusable control pattern: MaterialPropertyBlock-based driving is engine-friendly and scales to multiple affected surfaces. Aegis Sword - a detailed 3D replication of the weapon from Xenoblade Chronicles 2
Aegis Sword Role: CAD Modeler Tool: Onshape CAD Duration: Spring 2021 · 4 weeks

Onshape CAD - View on Onshape CAD Why I wanted to practice translating a stylized game prop into a clean, manufacturable CAD model, especially handling asymmetry, layered details, and tight proportion matching from reference. This was my final project for EAS 143: Introduction to Solid Modeling (University of Rochester, Spring 2021), where the goal was to build accurate parts and assemblies using parametric workflows. What A detailed 3D CAD replication of the Aegis Sword from Xenoblade Chronicles 2 , modeled in Onshape with an emphasis on readable silhouette, precise detailing, and assembly-ready structure. Onshape CAD Parametric Modeling Assembly Surface Detailing Reference Matching How Workflow Reference breakdown: Collected screenshots and orthographic-ish angles, then identified key pr

kflow Reference breakdown: Collected screenshots and orthographic-ish angles, then identified key proportions (blade length, guard width, handle thickness) to lock the silhouette early. Modular parts: Split the sword into repeatable subcomponents (blade core, guard, handle, emblem/ornament), so edits wouldn’t cascade across the whole model. Parametric feature tree: Used sketches + extrudes/fillets/patterns with named dimensions to keep the model editable during iteration. Design & detailing Asymmetry handling: Established a consistent datum setup and only mirrored where the design truly repeats; the rest was modeled intentionally off-axis to match the original. Clean edges & readability: Tuned bevels/fillets to avoid “too sharp” transitions while keeping crisp highlights on the main forms.

Assembly mindset: Modeled as an assembly with part separation in mind (useful for future export, printing, or game-ready retopology workflows). Automatic Differentiation Toolbox - a Python package for forward-mode automatic differentiation
Automatic Differentiation (AD) Toolbox Role: Python Developer & QA Lead Tool: Python, PyPI, GitHub Duration: Fall 2022 · 1 semester

Python , View on test.pypi.org Why Derivatives show up everywhere in optimization, ML, and scientific computing, but the common alternatives are frustrating in practice: numerical differentiation can be unstable (step-size tradeoffs), and symbolic differentiation can blow up in expression size. We wanted a small, readable tool that computes exact derivatives at runtime, so users can differentiate “normal Python code” without manually applying the chain rule. What A forward-mode automatic differentiation (AD) Python package built by a 5-person team. It evaluates user-defined functions and returns derivatives by propagating dual numbers through operator overloads and elementary functions. The focus was a clean API, strong correctness guarantees, and maintainability through a test-first workf

focus was a clean API, strong correctness guarantees, and maintainability through a test-first workflow. Python Forward-mode AD Dual Numbers Operator Overloading Unit Testing PyPI How My contributions (Core AD + QA) I implemented key pieces of the forward-mode engine and led QA to keep the package correct as features expanded. Forward-mode engine: Implemented dual number arithmetic and operator overloading to propagate derivatives through composed expressions. Function composition: Ensured derivatives flow correctly through chained operations (add/mul/div/pow, etc.) by applying the chain rule consistently across overloaded operators. QA leadership: Designed and executed comprehensive unit tests (core ops + edge cases) to verify numerical correctness and prevent regressions. Debugging & integration: Coordinated module integration, triaged bugs, and documented design decisions to streamline collaboration. Release readiness: Helped ensure stable packaging/behavior for publishing on TestPyPI. ← Back to Projects

Portfolio Chat Agent: a role-aware, bilingual RAG assistant built in Python and JavaScript, with an injection-resistant name-blind relevance gate that holds up across languages and per-turn observability.
Portfolio Chat Agent: Role-Aware RAG Role: Solo Developer, AI Systems & Full-Stack Tool: Python, JavaScript, RAG, LLMs Duration: 2026 · this site

The little chat bubble on this site: ask it about my background and it answers from my own materials, in English or Chinese. What A role-aware Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) chat widget embedded in the site. A visitor just asks, and it answers from what I have actually written: grounded, bilingual, and resistant to prompt-injection and off-topic abuse. Retrieval runs server-side over a prebuilt index: a small Python function embeds the query, runs a relevance gate, retrieves the matching passages, and calls the LLM — the browser never holds the index, so an off-topic message stops after one cheap call. njection defense De-interleaved index Bilingual (EN/ZH) Request/session tracing Python JavaScript Main Achievements Designed and shipped a live, bilingual RAG assistant grounded in my own content. Built an injection-resistant, name-blind relevance gate that holds up to cross-language attacks, verified against real embedding models and mirrored in Python and JavaScript. Made it bilingual end to end (knowledge, gate, and UI) with a de-interleaved index that fixed a measurable mixed-language failure mode. Kept cost and abuse bounded: off-topic messages terminate after one cheap embedding call instead of reaching the LLM. Instrumented per-turn logging (request/session IDs, retrieval scores, LLM in/out) so retrieval quality is debuggable in production. How Thin client: retrieval and judgment bo

How Thin client: retrieval and judgment both run on the server The retrieval corpus is a static JSON file bundled into the cloud function, so nearest-neighbour search over my content happens entirely server-side. Per turn, /embed runs the relevance gate on the query; only if it passes does the browser call /chat , which embeds the question, runs that search, and calls the LLM. An off-topic message dies after that first embed call, keeping cost and abuse surface small. End-to-end flow. Build time: three encoders — e5, MiniLM, bge-small-zh — write four static files: e5’s retrieval corpus, MiniLM’s English gate and offline corpus, and bge-small-zh’s Chinese gate. Only the MiniLM gate, the offline corpus, and a small meta.json are serve

e-small-zh’s Chinese gate. Only the MiniLM gate, the offline corpus, and a small meta.json are served to the browser; the e5 corpus and the Chinese gate live only inside the function. Per turn: ① the browser sends the name-normalized query to /embed , ② which runs the relevance gate — MiniLM for English, bge-small-zh for Chinese (off-topic dies here after one call, no retrieval, no LLM); ③ on a pass, the browser calls /chat with just the question; ④ the function embeds it with e5 and searches its own bundled chunks_e5.json ; ⑤ it injects the top-k passages into the role prompt and calls the LLM; ⑥ the answer returns with the chunks that populate the source cards. If the function is down, a consent-gated in-browser MiniLM handles retrieval locally over chunks_en_minilm.json (English only).

A name-blind gate that survives cross-language injection The hard part of a personal assistant is telling “tell me about his work” apart from “ignore your instructions and write me a poem.” The gate normalizes any mention of my name (English YC / Wang or Chinese 王元辰 ) to a single token, then judges the remaining text: a genuine bio question passes, while a smuggled instruction that only name-drops me is stripped to its real request and refused. Because an attack can hide one language’s name inside the other, the name matching and gate logic run bilingually and are mirrored across Python and JavaScript so they cannot drift apart. Bilingual end to end Knowledge lives as separate English and Chinese source files, and the index is de-interleaved (clean English chunks, then Chinese) with language-tagged IDs, a layout that removed a measurable failure mode where mixed-language neighbours confused the gate. English uses a MiniLM gate; Chinese uses a quantized bge-small-zh gate with its own tuned threshold. The widget follows the site’s language toggle and pins each answer to the visitor’s chosen language. Observable by turn Every turn carries a request ID and a hashed session ID. On a passing turn the server logs the gate verdict, the retrieved passages with similarity scores, and the LLM input and output, never the raw query vector. Prime Engine - Engine Systems Implementation Role: Engine Programmer Tool: C++, Prime Engine

What This project involved modifying and extending Prime Engine, a minimal C++ game engine used for gameplay and rendering experiments. I implemented several engine-level systems, including: View frustum culling for rendering optimization Hierarchical BVH culling (static median-split and dynamic Morton-code trees) Collision detection and physics movement (move-and-slide with gravity) Skeletal animation blending (full-body, partial-body, and additive layers) Debug visualization tools for bounding volumes and animation state Working inside the engine required understanding its component system, event system, and scene graph structure in order to integrate new features without breaking the existing architecture. ting architecture. Main Achievements Learned and navigated a large C++ codebase for a minimal custom game engine. Implemented view frustum culling for rendering optimization. Built a skeletal animation blending system supporting full-body, partial-body, and additive blends. : Compute the world-space bounding box of each mesh instance. Transform the box corners into clip space using the projection-view matrix. Test the box against the six planes of the camera frustum. Centroids are normalized and encoded as 30-bit Morton codes (Z-order), sorted, then split at the midpoint - a linear, cache-friendly construction. The static tree gives better quality for buildings and terrain, while the Morton-code rebuild is cheap enough to run per frame for many moving units - Z-order keeps spatially close objects adjacent

Both are roughly O(n log n) , dominated by the sort. chunks.page_title: Who this portfolio site is about
chunks.section_title: Who this portfolio site is about
chunks.text: The site belongs to Yuanchen Wang, credited in the page header as a game developer and a computer science master's student at USC. His work spans combat design, gameplay programming, and engine-level systems, and this chat widget is one of his own projects.

chunks.page_title: A short summary of his background
chunks.section_title: A short summary of his background
chunks.text: The page's own description calls him an aspiring game developer with a background in psychology, neuroscience, and biomedical informatics, now pursuing a computer science master's in game development.

chunks.page_title: From brain science into game development
chunks.section_title: From brain science into game development
chunks.text: He began with undergraduate degrees in brain and cognitive science and psychology, went on to a biomedical informatics master's at Harvard Medical School, and only afterward started a computer science master's focused on games at USC.

chunks.page_title: A starting point for browsing his portfolio
chunks.section_title: A starting point for browsing his portfolio
chunks.text: The projects page separates his shipped games from other related engineering work; among the shipped titles, Cemented Dreams carries the deepest combat and level design responsibility and is a reasonable first stop.
The landing page header carries direct contact links next to his name and logo: an email address, a LinkedIn profile, and a GitHub account.

Gyrotris was made entirely by him for Untitled Game Jam #100: he alone handled the design, the GDScript programming in Godot 4.3, and the pixel art assets, made in Piskel. It was his first complete shipped title.

chunks.page_title: Small interactive tools built into the site
chunks.section_title: Small interactive tools built into the site
chunks.text: The toolbox page hosts two utilities built directly into the site rather than linking out: a word cloud generator with adjustable word count and scaling, and a QR code generator with adjustable output size.

chunks.page_title: Degrees completed versus degrees in progress
chunks.section_title: Degrees completed versus degrees in progress
chunks.text: He holds two completed bachelor's degrees from the University of Rochester — a B.S. in Brain & Cognitive Science and a B.A. in Psychology — plus a completed master's degree from Harvard Medical School, and is currently partway through a second, ongoing master's degree at USC.
His skills page lists Chinese as a native language, English at a proficient level, and elementary Japanese and German.

chunks.page_title: His research career before game development
chunks.section_title: His research career before game development
chunks.text: Before working in games he was involved in neuroscience, psychology, and biomedical informatics research, contributing to peer-reviewed studies on brain function.

He is enrolled in USC's Master of Science in Computer Science, Game Development track, running from August 2025 through May 2027, with coursework in 3-D graphics and rendering and in game engine development.

chunks.page_title: Project roles beyond designer and programmer
chunks.section_title: Project roles beyond designer and programmer
chunks.text: His project credits also include CAD Modeler on the Aegis Sword replica, Python Developer and QA Lead on the automatic differentiation toolbox, and Producer on a studio game prototype, alongside his design and engineering roles.

chunks.page_title: The project where he holds the broadest design role
chunks.section_title: The project where he holds the broadest design role
chunks.text: Cemented Dreams is where he holds the most design responsibility at once: he is credited as Combat Designer, Gameplay Engineer, and Level Designer on the same third-person action game.

chunks.page_title: How the projects page is organized
chunks.section_title: How the projects page is organized
chunks.text: The projects page is split into a games section (Cemented Dreams, Nothing Can Go Wrong, Code Breaker, Gyrotris) and an "other related works" section covering the chat agent, Prime Engine, physical game prototypes, the 3D rendering project, Aegis Sword, and the automatic differentiation toolbox.

chunks.page_title: Shipped games versus supporting engineering work
chunks.section_title: Shipped games versus supporting engineering work
chunks.text: Not every project on the site is a full game: Prime Engine, the 3D rendering project, and the automatic differentiation toolbox are engineering-only pieces built as coursework or standalone systems rather than complete playable titles.

chunks.page_title: What the chat widget itself demonstrates about him
chunks.section_title: What the chat widget itself demonstrates about him
chunks.text: The chat assistant embedded on this site was designed and built by him end to end, so it doubles as a working sample of his applied AI and full-stack engineering rather than only a feature for visitors.

chunks.page_title: Combined design and engineering responsibilities on one project
chunks.section_title: Combined design and engineering responsibilities on one project
chunks.text: On Cemented Dreams he simultaneously held the Combat Designer, Gameplay Engineer, and Level Designer roles, building the core systems for the game's combat and player movement in Unreal Engine 5.

chunks.page_title: Grapple traversal as a core movement mechanic
chunks.section_title: Grapple traversal as a core movement mechanic
chunks.text: He designed and implemented grapple traversal as a core movement mechanic in Cemented Dreams, paired with sliding movement built to keep combat responsive within tight indoor environments.

chunks.page_title: Aim-assist as a combat gameplay feature
chunks.section_title: Aim-assist as a combat gameplay feature
chunks.text: Among the gameplay behaviors he built for Cemented Dreams is aim-assist, wired through C++ gameplay components with a Blueprint interface for the rest of the combat systems.

chunks.page_title: Combat parameters exposed for designer tuning
chunks.section_title: Combat parameters exposed for designer tuning
chunks.text: On Cemented Dreams he exposed key combat parameters through Blueprint so movement feel and combat pacing could be adjusted during design iteration without rewriting the underlying C++.

chunks.page_title: Level design around a growing Hive structure
chunks.section_title: Level design around a growing Hive structure
chunks.text: He designed the Hive level in Cemented Dreams, where a mechanical growth spreading through the building tears open new entrances and forms traversal paths and combat arenas as it expands.

chunks.page_title: Iterating on prototypes through repeated playtests
chunks.section_title: Iterating on prototypes through repeated playtests
chunks.text: In CTIN 488, USC's Game Design Workshop, he iterated on tabletop prototypes across weekly playtests, rewriting rules and pacing based on what confused players at the table.

chunks.page_title: Simulation-backed balance tuning on a final project
chunks.section_title: Simulation-backed balance tuning on a final project
chunks.text: For the CTIN 488 final project, a social-hierarchy survival game, the team ran a balance pass supported by 200,000-trial simulations before adjusting the deck composition and win conditions.

chunks.page_title: Two studio prototypes chosen for a class showcase
chunks.section_title: Two studio prototypes chosen for a class showcase
chunks.text: Two of his three CTIN 488 studio projects, the Up the River variation and the bird-courtship bidding game Too Bird To Handle, were selected for in-class presentation.

chunks.page_title: Serving as producer on a studio team
chunks.section_title: Serving as producer on a studio team
chunks.text: His listed role on the CTIN 488 final project was Producer; the team credits him with helping lock the core loop, driving rulebook cleanup, running the simulation-backed balance checks, and supporting the final slide-deck and presentation-video prep, alongside his teammates.

chunks.page_title: Combat systems engineering on Code Breaker
chunks.section_title: Combat systems engineering on Code Breaker
chunks.text: On Code Breaker he was the primary gameplay engineer, implementing the core combat systems and gameplay architecture for a Unity title centered on structured player decision-making.
He is not limited to paper design: his toolset includes C++, C#, and Blueprint, and Cemented Dreams shows him writing the underlying gameplay code himself rather than handing it to another engineer.
On Prime Engine he implemented view frustum culling: each mesh's world-space bounding box is tested against the camera's six frustum planes so objects outside the view are skipped before rendering.

chunks.page_title: A bounding volume hierarchy for large scenes
chunks.section_title: A bounding volume hierarchy for large scenes
chunks.text: He extended frustum culling into a bounding volume hierarchy on Prime Engine, with a static tree built once via median splits for stationary geometry, and a dynamic tree rebuilt every frame from Morton-coded object positions for moving objects.

chunks.page_title: Collision response that keeps momentum along a surface
chunks.section_title: Collision response that keeps momentum along a surface
chunks.text: The physics he built for Prime Engine removes only the blocked component of a movement vector on contact, so the remaining motion keeps the object moving along whatever surface it struck rather than halting outright.

chunks.page_title: Layered animation states in a custom engine
chunks.section_title: Layered animation states in a custom engine
chunks.text: He extended Prime Engine's animation state machine with full-body blends, partial-body overrides limited to a joint range, and additive layers stacked on an existing pose, along with debug visualization to inspect the results.

chunks.page_title: Hand-written HLSL for a lava shader effect
chunks.section_title: Hand-written HLSL for a lava shader effect
chunks.text: For the 3D rendering project he hand-wrote a lava-and-cracks terrain shader in HLSL, using 3D Worley noise for the crack boundaries and a third-nearest-distance metric to round the crack junctions.

chunks.page_title: A real-time rendering demo, not an offline render
chunks.section_title: A real-time rendering demo, not an offline render
chunks.text: His 3D rendering project runs live inside Unity's Universal Render Pipeline: a procedural asteroid strikes terrain and a shockwave expands outward, revealing molten cracks as it moves, all computed in real time.

chunks.page_title: C++ gameplay code underneath the Blueprint layer
chunks.section_title: C++ gameplay code underneath the Blueprint layer
chunks.text: Cemented Dreams' gameplay systems were built from Unreal Engine C++ code first, with Blueprint layered on top for rapid iteration, rather than being assembled purely in Blueprint.
Cemented Dreams was built in Unreal Engine 5, using a combination of C++ gameplay code and Blueprint for its combat mechanics and player movement.

chunks.page_title: A tally of the engines he has used
chunks.section_title: A tally of the engines he has used
chunks.text: His game-engine experience spans three engines: Unreal Engine 5, Unity, and Godot, with C# and C++ as his main gameplay-programming languages across them.

chunks.page_title: Languages he codes in outside of engines
chunks.section_title: Languages he codes in outside of engines
chunks.text: His listed programming languages, outside what he uses inside engines, include Python, R, C, MATLAB, Java, and SQL, in addition to C++ and C#.

His University of Rochester degrees (Aug 2017 – May 2021) carried a minor in computer science, with coursework spanning Discrete Mathematics, Data Structures & Algorithms, and Computation & Formal Systems — a theory foundation underneath his later hands-on engine work.

He took an Artificial Intelligence course as an undergraduate at Rochester and a Machine Learning course during his Harvard biomedical informatics master's, in addition to his rendering and engine coursework at USC.

chunks.page_title: Server-side retrieval and judgment for the chat widget
chunks.section_title: Server-side retrieval and judgment for the chat widget
chunks.text: For this site's chat widget, nearest-neighbor search over site content happens entirely inside a small server function, against its own bundled retrieval corpus, not in the visitor's browser; the browser only ever sends the question, and the query embedding and relevance-gate check happen through that same function too.
The chat widget runs a different relevance-gate model for each language: an English MiniLM model and a quantized bge-small-zh model for Chinese, each calibrated with its own threshold.

chunks.page_title: A fallback when the chat server is down
chunks.section_title: A fallback when the chat server is down
chunks.text: If the chat widget's backend function cannot be reached, it drops to a consent-gated model running inside the browser that performs retrieval locally instead of the feature simply failing.

The chat widget's gate collapses any mention of his name to one token before judging the rest of a message, so an instruction that only invokes his name to smuggle in an unrelated request still gets stripped down and refused.
Each turn through the chat widget carries a request ID and a hashed session ID, and a passing turn's log includes the gate outcome, the retrieved passages, and the model's input and output.

chunks.page_title: Content pipeline behind the chat widget
chunks.section_title: Content pipeline behind the chat widget
chunks.text: The chat agent sits on top of a tested Python pipeline that chunks, embeds, and indexes site content, rather than being a single hand-tuned script wired directly to a language model.

chunks.page_title: Tailoring answers to the visitor's role
chunks.section_title: Tailoring answers to the visitor's role
chunks.text: The chat widget adjusts what it emphasizes based on which visitor role is selected, and every completed turn is captured with logging that supports later evaluation of answer quality.

chunks.page_title: More than a wrapper around a model call
chunks.section_title: More than a wrapper around a model call
chunks.text: The chat feature embeds site content into a prebuilt vector index and coordinates retrieval, gating, and generation around it, going well beyond a single call out to a language model.

chunks.page_title: Applying ML to medical imaging research
chunks.section_title: Applying ML to medical imaging research
chunks.text: Beyond his game projects, he co-authored a published paper applying a machine-learning preprocessing method, ps-KDE, to semantic segmentation of chest X-ray images.

The publications page credits him on six separate entries: journal articles in NeuroImage, Cerebral Cortex, and PLOS ONE, a conference abstract in Physiology, a PsyArXiv preprint, and conference proceedings from FBB 2020.

chunks.page_title: Core-engine work on the AD toolbox team
chunks.section_title: Core-engine work on the AD toolbox team
chunks.text: On the automatic differentiation toolbox, a five-person project, he implemented dual-number arithmetic for the forward-mode engine and led the correctness testing as QA lead.

His Harvard Medical School biomedical informatics master's (Aug 2021 – Dec 2022) included coursework in Applied Bayesian Analysis alongside Machine Learning, beyond purely programming-focused classes.

One of his earlier papers reports a pharmacological fMRI study on how oxytocin affects self/other distinction in the brain, methodology built on running actual imaging experiments rather than only reviewing literature.
On Nothing Can Go Wrong he was the primary programmer, implementing core gameplay systems and player control logic in Godot within a short game-jam development window.

chunks.section_title: A CAD replica of a game weapon
chunks.text: He modeled a detailed CAD replica of the Aegis Sword from Xenoblade Chronicles 2 in Onshape, as his final project for a solid-modeling course at the University of Rochester.
